items.en: The Eight Recollections: Purpose, and the Buddha, Dharma, Saṃgha, Precepts
items.zh: 八念 · 教門所為 · 念佛念法念僧念戒

zh: 次釋八念法門。所言八念者：一、念佛；二、念法；三、念僧；四、念戒；五、念捨；六、念天；七、念入出息；八、念死。此八通稱念者，一心緣中，憶持不忘失故，名之為念。今釋八念，即為三意：一、明教門所為；二、明修證；三、明趣道之相。
en: Next, explaining the dharma-gate of the eight recollections. The eight recollections are: first, recollection of the Buddha; second, recollection of the Dharma; third, recollection of the Saṃgha; fourth, recollection of the precepts; fifth, recollection of relinquishment; sixth, recollection of the heavens; seventh, recollection of the breath entering and leaving; eighth, recollection of death. These eight are, in general, named recollection because, the mind fixed one-pointedly upon its object, one holds it in mind without forgetting or losing it — hence they are named recollection.

Explaining the eight recollections now has three senses: first, clarifying the purpose of this teaching-gate; second, clarifying their cultivation and realization; third, clarifying the mark of how they lead toward the path.

zh: 一、明教門所為者，佛弟子於阿蘭若處：空舍、塚間、山林、曠野，善修九想外不淨，厭患其身，而作是念：「我云何將是底下不淨臭屎尿囊以自隨逐？」爾時㱇然驚怖，舉身毛豎；及為惡魔作種種形色來恐怖之，欲令其道退沒。以是故念佛。次九想後，說八念，以除怖畏。如經中說：「佛告諸比丘：若於阿蘭若處有驚怖心，爾時應當念佛，恐怖即滅；若不念佛，應當念法，恐怖即除；若不念法，應當念僧，恐怖即除。」故知三念為除怖畏說也。
en: First, clarifying the purpose of this teaching-gate: the Buddha's disciple, dwelling in a forest hermitage — an empty dwelling, a charnel ground, mountain forest, or open wilderness — skillfully cultivates the nine contemplations' own external impurity, growing weary of and averse to his own body, and reflects thus: "How is it that I go about dragging along this very bag of base impurity, this stinking filth of excrement and urine, wherever I go?" At that moment, he is suddenly seized with terror, every hair on his body standing on end; and evil māras, too, taking on all manner of forms, come to terrify him further still, wishing thereby to make him retreat and fall back from the path. It is for this reason that recollection of the Buddha is taught. Following the nine contemplations, the eight recollections are thus taught, in order to remove this very fear. As the sutra says: "The Buddha told the monks: should fear and terror arise in the forest hermitage, one should, at that time, recollect the Buddha, and the fear is thereupon extinguished; should one not recollect the Buddha, one should recollect the Dharma, and the fear is thereupon removed; should one not recollect the Dharma, one should recollect the Saṃgha, and the fear is thereupon removed." Hence one knows that these first three recollections are taught specifically to remove fear and terror.

zh: 問曰：經說三念因緣為除怖畏，後五念復云何？答曰：是比丘自布施、持戒，怖畏即除。所以者何？若彼破戒，畏墮地獄；若慳貪，畏墮餓鬼及貧窮中，自念：「我有是淨戒、布施，則歡喜。上諸天皆是布施、持戒果報，我亦有是福德。」是故念天亦能令怖畏不生。十六行中，念阿那波那時，細心覺尚滅，何況怖畏麁覺？念死者，念五陰身念念生滅，從生已來，恒與死俱，今何以畏死？是五念，佛雖不別說，當知是為深除怖畏。所以者何？念他功德以除恐怖則難，念自功德以除怖畏則易。以是義故，不別說。
en: Question: the sutra explains that these three recollections' own causes and conditions are for removing fear and terror — what, then, of the latter five recollections? Answer: this is because the monk, through his own giving and precept-keeping, has his fear thereupon removed as well. Why is this? Should he have broken the precepts, he fears falling into hell; should he be stingy and greedy, he fears falling among the hungry ghosts or into poverty. Reflecting to himself: "I possess this very purity of precepts and giving" — he is thereupon filled with joy — "every heavenly being above is likewise the fruit of giving and precept-keeping, and I, too, possess this same merit." Hence recollection of the heavens, too, is able to keep fear from arising. Within the sixteen practices, at the moment of recollecting the breath entering and leaving, even the subtlest initial thought is extinguished — how much more so, then, the coarse initial thought of fear? As for recollection of death: recollecting that the body of the five aggregates arises and ceases moment after moment, and that, ever since birth, one has always been accompanied by death — why, then, should one fear death now? These five recollections, though the Buddha did not explain them separately, should be understood as likewise deeply removing fear. Why is this? Recollecting another's merit in order to remove fear is difficult, while recollecting one's own merit in order to remove fear is easy — for this reason, they were not explained separately.

zh: 二、明修證八念。念佛者，若行者於阿蘭若中，心有怖畏，應當念佛，佛是多陀阿伽度、阿羅訶、三藐三佛陀乃至婆伽婆，十號具足，三十二相、八十種好、大慈大悲、十力、四無所畏、十八不共法，智慧光明，神通無量，能度無量十方眾生，是我大師，救護一切，我當何畏？一心憶念，恐怖即除。
en: Second, clarifying the cultivation and realization of the eight recollections. Recollection of the Buddha: should the practitioner, within the forest hermitage, find fear arising in the mind, he should recollect the Buddha — the Buddha is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Fully and Perfectly Awakened One, all the way through to the World-Honored One, complete with the ten epithets; possessed of the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, great loving-kindness and great compassion, the ten powers, the four kinds of fearlessness, and the eighteen exclusive qualities; his wisdom's own light and supernormal powers beyond measure, able to deliver across countless beings throughout the ten directions. He is my own great teacher, the one who rescues and protects all — of what, then, should I be afraid? Recollecting one-pointedly in this way, fear is thereupon removed.

zh: 二、念法者，行者應念是法巧出，得今世果，無諸熱惱，不待時，能到善處，通達無礙。巧出者，善說二諦，不相違故，是法能出二邊，故名巧出。得今世果者，諸外道法皆無今世果，唯佛法中因緣展轉生。所謂持戒清淨故，得心不悔；得心不悔故，生法歡喜；生法歡喜故，得心樂；得心樂故，則能攝心；攝心故，得如實智；得如實智故，得厭離；得厭離故，得離欲；離欲故，得解脫；解脫果報故，得涅槃。是名得今世果報。無熱惱者，無三毒、生死熱惱也。不待時者，諸外道受法要須待時節，佛法不爾，譬如薪遇火即然，不待時。到善處者，若行佛法，必至人天樂果，三乘涅槃之處。通達無礙者，得三法印故，通達無礙也。我修如是等法，當何所畏？一心憶念，恐怖即除。
en: Second, recollection of the Dharma: the practitioner should recollect that this Dharma is skillfully liberating, yields its fruit already in this very life, is free of every feverish affliction, requires no waiting upon time, is able to arrive at a good place, and penetrates without obstruction.

"Skillfully liberating" means that it skillfully expounds the two truths without their contradicting each other, this very Dharma thereby able to transcend both extremes — hence it is named skillfully liberating. "Yields its fruit already in this very life" means that every non-Buddhist teaching lacks any fruit in this very life, while only within the Buddhadharma do causes and conditions unfold one from another in succession: that is, through the purity of upholding the precepts, one obtains freedom from remorse of mind; through freedom from remorse of mind, one gives rise to joy in the Dharma; through joy in the Dharma, one obtains happiness of mind; through happiness of mind, one is thereby able to gather in the mind; through gathering in the mind, one obtains wisdom that accords with reality; through wisdom that accords with reality, one obtains weariness and detachment; through weariness and detachment, one obtains freedom from desire; through freedom from desire, one obtains liberation; and through the fruit of liberation, one obtains nirvāṇa. This is named obtaining the fruit already in this very life.

"Free of every feverish affliction" means free of the three poisons and the feverish affliction of birth-and-death. "Requires no waiting upon time" means that, in receiving every non-Buddhist teaching, one must wait upon the proper time and season, while the Buddhadharma is not so — like firewood, which, meeting fire, ignites at once, without waiting upon any season. "Able to arrive at a good place" means that, practicing the Buddhadharma, one is certain to arrive at the happy fruit of the human and heavenly realms, and at the place of the three vehicles' own nirvāṇa. "Penetrates without obstruction" means that, having obtained the three dharma-seals, one penetrates without any obstruction whatsoever. I cultivate dharmas such as these — of what, then, should I be afraid? Recollecting one-pointedly in this way, fear is thereupon removed.

zh: 三、念僧者，行者應念僧，僧是佛弟子眾，具五分法身。是中有四雙八輩、二十七人，應受供養禮事，世間無上福田。所謂若聲聞僧、若辟支佛僧、若菩薩僧，神智無量，能救苦難，度脫眾生，如是聖眾，是我真伴，當何所畏？一心憶念，恐怖即除。四、念戒者，行者應念：是戒能遮諸惡，安隱住處。是中戒有二種，所謂有漏戒、無漏戒。復有二種：一、律儀戒；二、定共戒。律儀戒，能遮諸惡，身得安隱；定共戒，能遮諸煩惱，心得內樂；無漏戒，能破無明諸惡根本，得解脫樂。我修如是之法，當何所畏？一心憶念，恐怖即除。
en: Third, recollection of the Saṃgha: the practitioner should recollect the Saṃgha — the Saṃgha is the assembly of the Buddha's own disciples, complete with the five-part dharma-body. Among them are the four pairs and eight kinds of noble persons, and the twenty-seven kinds of persons, worthy of receiving offerings and reverent service, the world's own unsurpassed field of merit — whether the saṃgha of śrāvakas, the saṃgha of pratyekabuddhas, or the saṃgha of bodhisattvas, their spiritual wisdom beyond measure, able to rescue beings from suffering and hardship and deliver them across. Noble assemblies such as these are my own true companions — of what, then, should I be afraid? Recollecting one-pointedly in this way, fear is thereupon removed.

Fourth, recollection of the precepts: the practitioner should recollect that these precepts are able to block every evil, a place of peace and security to abide within. Among these precepts there are two kinds, namely the defiled precepts and the undefiled precepts. There are, further, two more kinds: first, the precepts of moral restraint; second, the precepts joined with concentration. The precepts of moral restraint are able to block every evil, the body thereby obtaining peace; the precepts joined with concentration are able to block every affliction, the mind thereby obtaining inner happiness; the undefiled precepts are able to break through ignorance, the root of every evil, obtaining thereby the happiness of liberation. I cultivate a dharma such as this — of what, then, should I be afraid? Recollecting one-pointedly in this way, fear is thereupon removed.

The eight recollections are presented as a direct sequel to the nine contemplations' own psychological aftermath — having deliberately induced revulsion toward the body, the text is candid that fear, not just detachment, is a predictable side effect, and even names evil māras seizing the moment to exploit that fear. The explanation for why only the first three recollections (Buddha, Dharma, Saṃgha) are explicitly framed around fear-removal in the source sutra, while the remaining five are not, is a small window into this treatise's own interpretive method: rather than simply reporting the canonical list, it reasons out why the sutra's own silence about the latter five still implies the same function — recollecting one's own merit is "easy," recollecting another's is "difficult," so the fear-removing five needed no separate explanation.

items.en: The Eight Recollections: Relinquishment, Heavens, Breath, Death — and the Path
items.zh: 八念 · 念捨念天念息念死 · 趣道

zh: 五、念捨者，行者應念捨有二種：一者、捨施捨；二者、諸煩惱捨。捨施有二種：一者、捨財；二者、捨法。是二種捨，皆名為捨，即是一切善法根本。行者自念：我有身已來亦有如是捨施功德，我當何畏？一心憶念，怖畏即除。六、念天者，行者應念：四天王天乃至他化自在天，彼諸天等悉因往昔戒施善根，得生彼處，長夜快樂，善法護念我等。復當憶念：天有四種：一者、名天；二者、生天；三者、淨天；四者、義生天。如是等天，果報清淨，若我有戒施之善，捨命之時，必生彼處，當何所畏？一心憶念，恐怖即除。
en: Fifth, recollection of relinquishment: the practitioner should recollect that relinquishment is of two kinds: first, the relinquishment of giving; second, the relinquishment of every affliction. The relinquishment of giving is, itself, of two kinds: first, the giving of wealth; second, the giving of the Dharma. Both of these two kinds of giving alike are named relinquishment, and are themselves the root of every wholesome dharma. The practitioner reflects to himself: ever since I have had this body, I have likewise possessed this very merit of relinquishment and giving — of what, then, should I be afraid? Recollecting one-pointedly in this way, fear is thereupon removed.

Sixth, recollection of the heavens: the practitioner should recollect that the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, all the way through to the Heaven of Free Enjoyment of Others' Transformations, and every heavenly being within them, alike obtained rebirth in these places entirely through their own wholesome root of precept-keeping and giving in past lives — enjoying happiness through the long night, their wholesome dharmas watching over and mindful of beings such as ourselves. One should further recollect that the heavens are of four kinds: first, the heavens in name only; second, the heavens of birth; third, the pure heavens; fourth, the heavens of meaning-born beings. Heavens such as these bear a pure fruit of retribution — should I, too, possess this very goodness of precept-keeping and giving, then, at the moment life is relinquished, I am certain to be born in a place such as these — of what, then, should I be afraid? Recollecting one-pointedly in this way, fear is thereupon removed.

zh: 七、念阿那波那者，如前六十特勝初門中說。行者若心驚怖，即當調息，緣息出入，覺知滿十，即當發言，念阿那波那，如是至十，六神即歸。一心念息，恐怖即除。次念死者，死有二種：一者、自死；二、他因緣死。是二種死，常隨此身，若他不殺，自亦當死，何足生怖？譬如勇士入陣，以死往遮，則心安無懼。如是一心念死，怖畏即除。是則略說八念對治恐怖。是中法相，並如《摩訶衍》廣分別。
en: Seventh, recollection of ānāpāna, the breath entering and leaving: as already explained in the opening gate of the sixteen special excellences above. Should the practitioner's own mind be seized with fear and terror, he should straightaway regulate the breath, taking the breath's own entering and leaving as his object, and, once aware of having counted a full ten breaths, should straightaway declare: "I recollect ānāpāna" — continuing thus up through ten, the six faculties thereupon return to their proper place. Recollecting the breath one-pointedly in this way, fear is thereupon removed.

Next, recollection of death: death is of two kinds: first, death of natural causes; second, death through others' causes and conditions. These two kinds of death, alike, are the constant companion of this very body — should others not kill me, I myself, too, must still die regardless: why, then, should this give rise to fear? It is like the brave warrior entering the field of battle, who, going forth to meet death itself head-on, thereby finds the mind at peace, without any fear at all. Recollecting death one-pointedly in just this way, fear is thereupon removed. This, then, briefly explains how the eight recollections counteract fear and terror; the dharma-characteristics involved here are all explained at greater length in the Mahāyāna treatise.

zh: 三、明八念趣道之相者，若如前說，止是權除怖畏及諸障難，今明善修八念，即是一途入道法門。釋八念入道有二意：一者、次第修行入道之相；二者、一一念各得入道。次第修行入道者，行者欲求解脫煩惱之病，先當念佛如醫王，念法如良藥，念僧如瞻病，念戒如禁忌飲食，念捨如將養，念天如身病少差，念阿那波那使發禪定，念死即悟無常四諦。若三界病盡，即得聖道。
en: Third, clarifying the mark of how the eight recollections lead toward the path: should one proceed as already explained above, this is merely a skillful means for removing fear and terror and every obstruction and difficulty; here, it is further clarified that skillfully cultivating the eight recollections is, in itself, a single path's own dharma-gate for entering the path.

Explaining how the eight recollections enter the path has two senses: first, the mark of entering the path through sequential cultivation; second, each single recollection, on its own, being able to lead to entering the path.

As for entering the path through sequential cultivation: the practitioner, wishing to seek liberation from the illness of affliction, should first recollect the Buddha as the king of physicians, recollect the Dharma as the fine medicine, recollect the Saṃgha as the one who attends the sick, recollect the precepts as the forbidden foods to be avoided, recollect relinquishment as the nourishing care that follows, recollect the heavens as the body's illness beginning to improve, recollect ānāpāna as that which brings forth dhyāna concentration itself, and recollect death as awakening to impermanence and the Four Noble Truths. Once the illness belonging to the three realms is entirely exhausted, one thereupon obtains the noble path.

zh: 二者、明一一念各是入道方法者，念佛，即是念佛三昧入道之相，如《文殊般若》及諸經中說。念法者，如經說：「諸佛所師，所謂法也。」若四諦、十二因緣、六波羅蜜、中道、實相，如是等法，皆是入道之法。念僧者，如《觀世音》、《三昧》、《藥上》等經中說。念戒，如前十種戒中說。念施，如《摩訶衍》中檀波羅蜜入道相中說。餘三念者，若念天及第一義天，即入道；若念阿那波那入道之相，具如通明中說；念死，如下死想義中說。當知八念，隨修一念即得入道，不須餘習。菩薩為求佛道故，行是八念，心無依倚，大悲方便，廣習法門以化眾生。當知八念即是菩薩摩訶衍也。
en: Second, clarifying how each single recollection, on its own, is itself a method for entering the path: recollection of the Buddha is precisely the mark of entering the path through the samādhi of buddha-recollection, as explained in the Mañjuśrī-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra and throughout the other scriptures. Recollection of the Dharma is as the sutra says: "That which every buddha takes as teacher is precisely the Dharma itself" — the Four Noble Truths, the twelve links of dependent origination, the six pāramitās, the middle way, and true reality: dharmas such as these are, every one, a method of entering the path. Recollection of the Saṃgha is as explained in the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra, the Samādhi Sūtra, the Bhaiṣajyarāja Sūtra, and the rest. Recollection of the precepts is as already explained above, among the ten kinds of precepts. Recollection of giving is as explained in the Mahāyāna treatise, within the mark of entering the path through the dāna-pāramitā.

As for the remaining three recollections: recollection of the heavens, and of the heaven of ultimate meaning, is likewise a path of entry; the mark of entering the path through recollection of ānāpāna is given in full within the thorough-and-bright contemplation, already explained above; and recollection of death is as explained below, within the sense of the perception of death.

One should know, then, that, among the eight recollections, cultivating even a single one of them is already sufficient to enter the path, without any need for further practice besides. The bodhisattva, seeking buddhahood, practices these eight recollections with a mind that rests upon and clings to nothing, employing great compassion's own skillful means, broadly cultivating every dharma-gate in order to transform sentient beings. One should know, then, that the eight recollections are themselves precisely the bodhisattva's own Mahāyāna.

The medical simile organizing the sequential path — Buddha as physician, Dharma as medicine, Saṃgha as caregiver, precepts as dietary restriction, relinquishment as convalescent care, the heavens as early recovery, the breath as what brings forth dhyāna concentration, death as awakening to impermanence and the Four Noble Truths — gives the eight recollections a narrative arc the nine contemplations didn't have: a full course of treatment, not just a repeated antidote. The second framing, that any single recollection independently opens the same door, is the more radical claim, and the text backs it with citations across a wide range of other scriptures (the Mañjuśrī-prajñāpāramitā, the Avalokiteśvara and Bhaiṣajyarāja sūtras) — suggesting each of the eight recollections already had its own, separately developed devotional tradition that this treatise is here folding into a single unified scheme.

quiz.q: What are the eight recollections, in order?
options: Buddha, Dharma, Saṃgha, precepts, relinquishment, heavens, the breath, death
quiz.why: The eight are recollection of the Buddha, Dharma, Saṃgha, precepts, relinquishment, heavens, the breath, and death.

quiz.q: Why are the eight called "recollections"?
options: the mind fixed on its object, holding it without forgetting
quiz.why: With the mind fixed one-pointedly on its object, one holds it without forgetting, hence "recollection."

quiz.q: Why are the eight recollections taught after the nine contemplations?
options: practicing the nine in the forest, one is seized by terror and harassed by Māra, so the eight remove fear
quiz.why: Weary of the body through the nine, the practitioner is suddenly terrified, hair on end, and Māra appears to frighten him; the eight recollections remove this fear.

quiz.q: According to the sūtra, what should a frightened monk in the forest recollect, in order?
options: the Buddha, else the Dharma, else the Saṃgha
quiz.why: One should recollect the Buddha; failing that, the Dharma; failing that, the Saṃgha, and the fear is removed.

quiz.q: The sūtra names only the first three for removing fear. Why did the Buddha not separately mention the latter five?
options: recollecting another's merit is hard; recollecting one's own is easy
quiz.why: Recollecting another's merit to remove fear is difficult, recollecting one's own is easy; so the latter five need not be stated separately.

quiz.q: Why does recollecting the breath keep fear from arising?
options: even subtle thought ceases, how much more the coarse thought of fear
quiz.why: When recollecting the breath, even subtle thought is extinguished, how much more the coarse thought of fear.

quiz.q: What qualities of the Buddha are recollected?
options: ten epithets, thirty-two marks, eighty features, great compassion, ten powers, four fearlessnesses, eighteen exclusive qualities
quiz.why: One recollects the ten epithets, thirty-two marks, eighty features, great compassion, ten powers, four fearlessnesses, and eighteen exclusive qualities: he is my teacher, so what should I fear?

quiz.q: In recollecting the Dharma, what does "skillfully liberating" mean?
options: it expounds the two truths without contradiction, transcending both extremes
quiz.why: It expounds the two truths skillfully without contradiction and so transcends both extremes. C and D are other qualities.

quiz.q: Which step of the chain "fruit in this very life" is correct?
options: pure precepts, no remorse, joy, happiness, concentration, true knowledge, disenchantment, dispassion, liberation, nirvāṇa
quiz.why: Pure precepts bring freedom from remorse, then joy, happiness, a gathered mind, knowledge according with reality, disenchantment, dispassion, liberation, and nirvāṇa.

quiz.q: With what is the Dharma's "requiring no waiting upon time" compared?
options: firewood igniting as soon as it meets fire
quiz.why: Non-Buddhist teachings must wait for proper seasons, but the Buddhadharma is like firewood that ignites as soon as it meets fire.

quiz.q: What does the Saṃgha possess, and which three saṃghas are named?
options: the five-part dharma-body; śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, and bodhisattva saṃghas
quiz.why: The Saṃgha, complete with the five-part dharma-body, includes śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas, my true companions.

quiz.q: What does each of the three kinds of precepts do?
options: restraint blocks evil, giving bodily peace; concentration-joined blocks afflictions, giving inner happiness; undefiled breaks ignorance, giving liberation
quiz.why: Moral-restraint precepts block evil, giving bodily peace; concentration-joined precepts block afflictions, giving inner happiness; undefiled precepts break ignorance, giving liberation.

quiz.q: What are the two kinds of relinquishment, and the two kinds of giving?
options: relinquishment of giving and of afflictions; giving wealth and giving Dharma
quiz.why: Relinquishment is of giving and of afflictions; giving is of wealth and of the Dharma, the root of all wholesome dharmas.

quiz.q: Why does recollecting one's own giving and precepts remove fear?
options: one fears hell or ghost-realms from broken precepts and greed; knowing one has pure precepts and giving brings joy
quiz.why: Broken precepts bring fear of hell, stinginess fear of the ghost realm; knowing one has pure precepts and giving brings joy, since the heavens are the fruit of these.

quiz.q: In recollecting the heavens, what four kinds of heaven are named?
options: heavens in name, of birth, pure, and meaning-born
quiz.why: The four are the heavens in name, of birth, pure heavens, and meaning-born heavens.

quiz.q: How does recollecting the breath remove fear?
options: regulate the breath, count to ten, declare "I recollect ānāpāna," and the six faculties return
quiz.why: When frightened, one regulates the breath and follows it; after a full ten, one says "I recollect ānāpāna," and continuing thus the six faculties return.

quiz.q: What two kinds of death are recollected, and what simile shows a fearless mind?
options: natural and caused by others; a brave warrior who meets death head-on is at peace
quiz.why: Death comes naturally or through others; if not killed, one still dies, so why fear? Like a warrior who goes to meet death head-on, the mind is at peace.

quiz.q: In recollecting the heavens, by what did the gods obtain rebirth there?
options: past wholesome roots of precepts and giving
quiz.why: The gods from the Four Kings through Paranirmita-vaśavartin were born there through past precepts and giving; having the same, one is sure to be reborn there.

quiz.q: In the sequential path, how are the eight compared to treating illness?
options: Buddha as physician, Dharma as medicine, Saṃgha as nurse, precepts as diet, relinquishment as nourishing care, heavens as improvement
quiz.why: The Buddha is the king of physicians, the Dharma medicine, the Saṃgha the nurse, precepts the dietary restrictions, relinquishment nourishing care, and the heavens the illness improving.

quiz.q: In the illness simile, what do recollecting the breath and death each do?
options: the breath brings forth dhyāna; death brings awakening to impermanence and the truths
quiz.why: Recollecting the breath brings forth dhyāna; recollecting death awakens one to impermanence and the Four Truths; when the illness of the three realms is gone, one attains the noble path.

quiz.q: When each recollection leads to the path, what does the sūtra say about recollecting the Dharma?
options: "what the buddhas take as teacher is the Dharma"
quiz.why: As the sūtra says, what the buddhas take as teacher is the Dharma; the truths, links, perfections, middle way, and true reality are all methods of entering the path.

quiz.q: What does the text conclude about the eight recollections and the path?
options: cultivating any one suffices; the bodhisattva practices them with compassion, and they are the Mahāyāna
quiz.why: Cultivating even one recollection suffices to enter the path; the bodhisattva practices all eight without clinging, with compassion, so they are the bodhisattva's Mahāyāna.
